Company scope (published): white-glove delivery means the item crosses the threshold — brought in on a planned route, set in its final position, packaging removed, and condition verified with the recipient before the crew leaves, never left at a curb. The work runs piece by piece, never bulk: each piece is assessed on its own — weight, fragile points, finish and value at risk — then protected to match: furniture and pieces travel fully covered in padded blankets and sealed with clear stretch wrap, and pieces that need more get a custom crate built around them. Antiques, art, pianos and instruments are the everyday work of this service. Behind the delivery sits the company's own final-mile chain — freight is received and counted on the warehouse floor, staged, deconsolidated or cross-docked, and reworked where needed, then delivered in by the crew that handled it, with no hand-off to an unknown last carrier. A high-value delivery of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs — a safe, a piano, medical equipment — is surveyed and floor-checked to L/360 under SIR Structural Integrity Relocation and the KIM-GS Protocol before it is scheduled. Every job is reviewed in full and quoted at one flat rate agreed in writing before dispatch; no rate schedule is published for this service. Guaranteed Flat Rate or Your Move is Free!

process.name: Item list and survey
process.text: The job starts as an item list — each piece named, with dimensions, weight where known, and the rooms they are bound for. The path is surveyed with it: stairs, turns, doorways, floor surfaces. High-value pieces are listed individually, with declared values, the way the federal paperwork will want them.

process.name: Level chosen in writing
process.text: The delivery level is chosen per job and written into the flat-rate quote before work begins: white glove in full, or a lower level where the piece honestly allows it. The quote states what the level includes, so the appointment holds no surprises.

process.name: Appointment window
process.text: The delivery runs to a scheduled appointment window, arranged around the customer, the building, or the designer's install day — not an all-day wait at the curb.

process.name: Protected carry-in
process.text: Floors and doorways on the path are protected before the first piece moves. Crew size follows the piece and the path from the survey — heavy or bulky pieces travel with two people, on the NIOSH arithmetic, never on hope.

process.name: Room-of-choice placement
process.text: Each piece goes to the room the customer names and is positioned to the plan — the customer's, or the designer's instructions where a designer is running the install.

process.name: Unpack, light assembly, joint inspection
process.text: Pieces are unpacked in the room, light assembly from the maker's kit is completed, and each piece is inspected together with the customer. Condition is noted on the delivery record while both parties are looking at the item.

process.name: Packaging out, sign-off
process.text: Every piece of packaging and debris leaves with the crew. The delivery record is signed against the item list, and the room is left finished — furniture standing, nothing to break down, nothing to haul.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — White-Glove Delivery Levels: Domain Reference Dataset
@graph.description: Domain reference — the delivery-level ladder the industry sells, labeled as domain vocabulary, and this company's published position on it. The level describes one thing: how far the crew carries the item. Curbside: the item is left at the curb or driveway. Threshold: the item is carried inside the first door, garage or lobby, no further. Room of choice: the item is carried to the room the recipient picks; unpacking is not included. Room of choice with packaging removal: placement in the room, and the packaging is taken away. White glove: room of choice plus unpacking, inspection with the recipient, and packaging and debris removal — brought in on a planned route, set in its final position, and condition verified with the recipient before the crew leaves. Some providers stack assembly or installation above white glove. The names are not standardized anywhere in the industry — no regulator defines them — so two quotes can both say white glove and deliver different rooms, different unpacking and different debris outcomes; the details confirmed in writing are worth more than the level named on a quote. The company's published position: The Flat Rate Movers publishes the top of the ladder as this service's standard — placed, unpacked and verified, never a curbside drop — and publishes no lower tier as this service's offer. Assembly and installation are named here as domain tier components only; they are not part of this company's published white-glove scope.

researchClaims.detail: The two levels are set by 49 CFR 375.701 (released value) and 375.703 (full value). For a high-value, low-weight piece — exactly the white-glove profile — the released-value formula returns almost nothing: the protection decision belongs in writing before the move, not after a claim.
researchClaims.fact: Federal rules give interstate household-goods customers two liability levels. Full Value Protection is the default: if an article is lost, destroyed, or damaged in the mover's custody, the mover must repair it, replace it with one of like kind, or pay its current market replacement value. Released Value — 60 cents per pound per article — applies only when the customer signs a specific statement choosing it on the bill of lading.
researchClaims.headline: On an interstate move, full value protection is the federal default
researchClaims.scope: Interstate household-goods moves under FMCSA jurisdiction; intrastate moves follow state law.

source.title: Before Requesting Services from Any Mover (Subpart B) — FMCSA Protect Your Move

researchClaims.detail: This is why a white-glove delivery starts with an item list, not a truck: the pieces that most need the careful service are the same pieces the paperwork must name individually, with their values, before custody changes hands.
researchClaims.fact: Under the federal full-value rules, an article of extraordinary value is any item worth more than $100 per pound — jewelry, silverware, china, furs, antiques, and artwork are the FMCSA's own examples. A mover may limit its liability for such an article unless the customer specifically lists it on the shipping documents.
researchClaims.headline: Items worth more than $100 per pound must be listed in writing
researchClaims.scope: Interstate household-goods moves; the $100-per-pound threshold and the listing rule are stated in 49 CFR 375.703(b) as FMCSA presents them.

source.title: Before Requesting Services from Any Mover (Subpart B) — FMCSA Protect Your Move

researchClaims.detail: The distinction decides who pays and how much after damage: a valuation claim runs against the carrier under the contract's liability level, while third-party insurance follows its own policy terms. Both can be in play on one delivery; they are never the same instrument.
researchClaims.fact: Valuation is the tariff-based level of carrier liability written into the moving contract; it is not an insurance policy and is not governed by state insurance law. FMCSA's consumer booklet states it directly: valuation is simply a tariff-based level of motor carrier liability.
researchClaims.headline: Valuation is not insurance — FMCSA says so in those words
researchClaims.scope: Federal framing for interstate household-goods carriage, quoted from FMCSA's own consumer guidance.

source.title: Frequently Asked Questions — FMCSA (liability and valuation)

researchClaims.detail: White-glove work is built around this arithmetic: the crew size is set by the piece and the path — weight, stairs, turns, doorways — at the survey, so the delivery day runs the plan instead of discovering it. The same constant anchors the estate's local-moving research layer (L2-LOC-OPS-01).
researchClaims.fact: NIOSH's lifting equation sets a load constant of 51 pounds under ideal conditions — the recommended weight limit is then reduced by posture, reach, frequency, and coupling multipliers. A piece above that constant, or bulky enough to wreck the multipliers, is a two-person carry as a matter of ergonomics, not preference.
researchClaims.headline: The 51-pound constant is why heavy pieces move with two people
researchClaims.scope: Ergonomic design guidance for manual lifting tasks; the 51 lb load constant is the equation's ideal-conditions starting point.

source.publisher: National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health
source.title: Applications Manual for the Revised NIOSH Lifting Equation (Publication No. 94-110)

researchClaims.detail: A white-glove delivery builds that inspection into the service itself — the piece is unpacked in the room and looked over with the customer present, so condition is recorded while both parties are looking at the same item in the same light.
researchClaims.fact: Federal consumer guidance puts the delivery moment at the center of protection: the customer inspects the goods at delivery and notes any damage or missing items on the delivery record before signing, because that notation is the contemporaneous evidence a later claim stands on.
researchClaims.headline: Condition is settled at the door, on the delivery record
researchClaims.scope: Interstate household-goods delivery practice as FMCSA instructs consumers; the same documentation discipline is sound practice on any high-value delivery.

source.title: Frequently Asked Questions — FMCSA (delivery and claims)

researchClaims.detail: Naming the line in the quote is what separates a defined service from a slogan: the customer knows which pieces will be standing finished at the end of the appointment and which tasks belong to other trades, before anyone is on site.
researchClaims.fact: Across the trade, white-glove assembly means the light assembly a furniture piece needs to stand and function — legs, sections, shelves, hardware from the maker's kit — performed in the room. It does not mean built-ins, anchoring into structure beyond the maker's instructions, or trades work such as plumbing and electrical hookups.
researchClaims.headline: Assembly in white glove means light assembly — the line is part of the service definition
researchClaims.scope: Industry scope definition for white-glove delivery services; company scope is set per job in the written quote.
